title: What Equipment Is Used to Clean Air Ducts?
h1: What Equipment Do Professionals Use to Clean Air Ducts?
description: Professional duct cleaning uses negative air machines, rotating brushes, air whips, cameras and HEPA vacuums. Here is what each tool does and why it matters.
quick_answer: Professional air duct cleaning uses a negative air machine to put the ducts under suction, agitation tools like rotating brushes and compressed-air whips to knock debris loose, HEPA vacuums for registers and equipment, and inspection cameras to see inside the ducts before and after. The key is pairing strong suction with agitation so debris gets pulled out instead of blown into the house.
body:
If you're getting quotes for duct cleaning, it helps to know what a real job looks like. The equipment tells you a lot. A shop vacuum held up to a register isn't duct cleaning. A proper cleaning reaches the whole system, from the return grilles to the supply registers, and the tools are built to do that.

What is a negative air machine?

This is the main piece of equipment in a professional cleaning. It's a powerful fan and collection system that connects to the duct system, usually at the main trunk or near the furnace or air handler. When it runs, it pulls air through the ducts toward the machine, so the whole system is under suction.

There are two common types:

  • Portable HEPA units that sit inside the home or garage and filter the air before releasing it
  • Truck-mounted units that stay outside with a large hose running into the house

Either can work well. What matters is that the system pulls enough air to carry debris out of the ducts and that the exhaust is filtered or sent outside.

What tools loosen the debris?

Suction alone won't clean ducts. Dust sticks to the walls, especially in older systems. Agitation tools knock it loose so the suction can carry it away:

  • Rotating brushes on long flexible cables that spin through the ducts. Different brush sizes and stiffness are used for metal and flex ducts.
  • Air whips, which are hoses with whipping ends powered by compressed air. They snap against the duct walls to dislodge debris.
  • Skipper balls and air nozzles, which are compressed-air tools that bounce or travel through the ducts, pushing dust toward the collection point.
  • Hand brushes and scrapers for registers, grilles and plenums that are easy to reach.

Flex duct, which is common in Southern California attics, needs gentler tools than sheet metal, since stiff brushes can tear the inner liner.

What other equipment is part of the job?

  • Inspection cameras. A camera on a cable shows what's inside before and after cleaning. You should be able to see the footage or photos.
  • HEPA vacuums. Used to clean registers, grilles, the blower area and the return plenum.
  • Air compressor. Powers the air whips and other agitation tools.
  • Register covers and plastic sheeting. Seal off openings so dust doesn't escape into rooms while the system is under suction.
  • Access tools. Used to cut and then properly seal access points in sheet metal ducts where needed.
  • Fogging equipment. Used to apply a sanitizer or deodorizer if you choose that service. Products should be EPA-registered for use in HVAC systems.

How do the tools work together?

A typical cleaning follows this order:

  1. Inspect the system with a camera and take photos.
  2. Cover the supply registers and connect the negative air machine.
  3. Turn on suction to put the ducts under negative pressure.
  4. Work through each supply and return line with agitation tools, one at a time.
  5. Clean the registers, grilles, return plenum and blower area.
  6. Apply sanitizer if requested.
  7. Seal access points, reinstall registers and inspect again.

What should I watch out for?

Be wary of very cheap offers that promise a whole-house cleaning in under an hour. Those jobs often skip the negative air machine or only clean the registers you can see. Ask what equipment will be used, whether the returns are included and whether you'll get before-and-after photos.

It is also fair to ask about the condition of your ducts before cleaning. If flex ducts in the attic are torn, crushed or falling apart, cleaning them may not be the best use of money. In that case, repair or replacement could make more sense, and an honest technician will tell you so after looking with a camera.

Our air duct cleaning service uses negative pressure, agitation tools and camera inspection, and includes the returns and registers. You can find current duct cleaning offers on our specials page.
faqs: Can I clean my air ducts with a regular vacuum?
A household vacuum can clean register covers and the first few inches of the duct. It can't reach deep into the system or create the suction needed to pull debris out of the whole duct run.
Does duct cleaning damage flex ducts?
It shouldn't when done right. Flex ducts need softer brushes and air tools rather than stiff rotating brushes. Badly damaged or very old flex duct may be better replaced than cleaned.
How long does professional duct cleaning take?
Most homes take a few hours, depending on the number of vents, the size of the system and how dirty it is. Very large or heavily contaminated systems can take longer.
Should I get my ducts sanitized?
Sanitizing can help after mold, rodent activity or strong odors. It isn't needed for every home. Ask what product is used and make sure it's registered for HVAC use.
